page: Microsoft Azure FX48-24mds_v2 is a specialized instance configured with constrained core licensing for workloads requiring high memory capacity and elevated per-core compute performance. Built on the x86_64 architecture, it is powered by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor operating at 4.2 GHz. The instance provisions 24 dedicated vCPUs across 12 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled, backed by a large 260 MB L3 cache, 2 MB L2 cache per core, and instruction set support for AVX-512 and Intel AMX. Bundled hardware resources include 1008.0 GB of system memory, yielding an extensive 42.0 GB per vCPU, along with 2832 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. There are no GPUs attached.

Benchmark evaluations demonstrate exceptional single-thread processing capabilities. The instance achieved a Geekbench single-core score of 2339.0 and a text processing score of 2938.0, both placing in the top 10 percent of tested servers. Multi-core performance is also robust, recording 16414.0 on Geekbench multi-core and 26642.26 on stress-ng. Memory throughput proves efficient under heavy load, reaching 186.82 GB/sec in uncached 256 MB read operations. File compression tasks perform strongly as well, demonstrated by single-threaded gzip compression at 34.71 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression at 14.24 GB/sec.

From a cost efficiency standpoint, this instance targets software deployments with per-core licensing restrictions, such as proprietary relational databases, where paying for excessive CPU cores would substantially increase software licensing fees. By pairing a restrained core count with over a terabyte of RAM and high-speed local NVMe scratch storage, the platform minimizes licensing overhead while avoiding memory bottlenecks. A trade-off is the absence of GPU acceleration, precluding heavy machine learning training workflows.

The hardware configuration is well-suited for large in-memory databases, electronic design automation (EDA), complex financial simulations, caching tiers like Redis, and compute jobs requiring high single-thread clock speeds alongside large active memory datasets.
